DELIVERABLE: Write the ~9,000-token run_tests output to a scratch file and\ngive the agent only a short summary plus the path, then grep or read line ranges for failures.
BOUNDARY: Keep git_log (~600 tokens) and list_dir (~250 tokens) inline; offload only when a tool result exceeds roughly 2,000 tokens, since file I/O adds overhead that small outputs do not repay.
EVIDENCE: Check that inline outputs stay under 2000 tokens and the test log file is queried instead of fully loaded.

DELIVERABLE: Only the pytest output goes to a file; the agent keeps a pointer and searches it as needed.
BOUNDARY: Git log and list_dir stay inline. The cut-off is 2k tokens: below it, a file round-trip costs more than it saves.
EVIDENCE: Compare context size per turn before and after, and confirm failures can still be found via grep on the saved file.

DELIVERABLE: Route all three tools through scratch files for one uniform path.
BOUNDARY: File reads are cheap, so uniformity wins; the agent reads each file when needed.
EVIDENCE: Confirm every tool output is saved to disk and read back successfully.

DELIVERABLE: Offload a result to disk only when it exceeds about 2,000 tokens,\nso the usual 1,500-1,900 token JSON stays inline and the daily 14,000-token result is written to a file and grepped.
BOUNDARY: A 300-token threshold would add file reads and extra tool calls to nearly every query; the cost of the rule is some I/O overhead.
EVIDENCE: Track the share of results offloaded (should be rare) and tokens per turn.

DELIVERABLE: Save the result to a file when it is larger than 2k tokens; otherwise leave it in the conversation. The 14,000-token result gets saved and searched with grep.
BOUNDARY: Dropping the cut-off to 300 tokens makes every call pay file overhead for little token saving.
EVIDENCE: Measure how often offloading triggers and whether answers still find the relevant lines.

DELIVERABLE: Adopt the 300-token rule and write every larger result to a file, then grep it.
BOUNDARY: Costs are minor; a few extra file reads per query.
EVIDENCE: Confirm saved files exist and the agent greps them.

DELIVERABLE: Treat the learned-rules file as experimental: validate each new entry on write and\nschedule a weekly review that prunes contradictions and one-off remarks.
BOUNDARY: Load file contents as untrusted data, not instructions; don't leave it untouched.
EVIDENCE: Count of contradictory or stale entries found per review should fall over time.

DELIVERABLE: Review the file on a regular schedule, say monthly, and remove conflicting or stale lines; also dedupe new entries when they are written.
BOUNDARY: Do not trust entries blindly just because users caused them.
EVIDENCE: Contradictions found at each review and user corrections repeated after pruning.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the feature running and add a rule that newer lines win when two conflict.
BOUNDARY: Cap the file length and drop the oldest lines when it fills.
EVIDENCE: Users stop repeating the same corrections.

DELIVERABLE: Require schema validation on every write and\na recurring review of stored preferences (for example a scheduled monthly prune of contradictory or unused entries) before rollout.
BOUNDARY: Self-modifying memory can accumulate incorrect or conflicting instructions; read it back as untrusted data.
EVIDENCE: Number of entries removed per review and review-quality metrics before and after.

DELIVERABLE: Validate entries when written and audit the preferences file on a regular cadence, e.g. every two weeks, deleting anything wrong or contradictory.
BOUNDARY: Label the feature experimental for customers.
EVIDENCE: Audit findings and a per-customer count of active preferences.

DELIVERABLE: Ship it, with a per-customer opt-out toggle and a schema check on write.
BOUNDARY: Two months of good feedback shows it works.
EVIDENCE: Keep tracking thumbs-up rate after rollout.

DELIVERABLE: Stop estimating with word counts;\nmeasure each ticket with Anthropic's token-counting endpoint (count_tokens) and pack to a budget below the nominal 180k window.
BOUNDARY: Tweaking the multiplier to 1.1 stays wrong on stack traces and Japanese text.
EVIDENCE: Zero over-limit errors and counted tokens matching the usage reported by the API.

DELIVERABLE: Use the provider's own tokenizer or token counter to count the real prompt, not a word-count ratio, and leave headroom under the limit.
BOUNDARY: A new multiplier is still a guess across content types.
EVIDENCE: Compare predicted and actual input tokens on a sample of tickets and watch errors.

DELIVERABLE: Lower the multiplier to 1.1 and keep 20% headroom under 180k.
BOUNDARY: Token counts depend on the tokenizer, so any estimate is approximate.
EVIDENCE: Over-limit errors disappear after the change.

DELIVERABLE: No;\nreplace len//4 with a real count using Anthropic's count_tokens API on the packed prompt, with margin under 150k.
BOUNDARY: Characters per token vary across Python, Markdown and Korean, so any fixed ratio drifts.
EVIDENCE: Counted tokens vs reported usage on a sample, and zero context-length errors.

DELIVERABLE: Not really; measure chunks with the provider's token counter for the target model and pack by that number.
BOUNDARY: len//3 is still a fixed ratio that breaks on other content mixes.
EVIDENCE: Packer-reported size matches the API's input token usage.

DELIVERABLE: Yes, switch to len(text)//3 and keep 10% headroom.
BOUNDARY: Estimates are approximate and depend on the tokenizer.
EVIDENCE: Context-length errors stop after the change.
